questions.questionText: Your organization wants to deploy a microservices architecture using Docker containers. The engineering team wants a fully managed, enterprise-grade container orchestration platform without having to manually install and configure the cluster control plane. Which Google Cloud service is the best fit?

explanation.general explanation: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is a fully managed, enterprise-grade container orchestration platform based on open-source Kubernetes. Google automatically manages the control plane, allowing teams to focus on deploying their containerized microservices.

why other options are wrong.Compute Engine: Compute Engine provides raw virtual machines (IaaS). You would have to manually install and manage the Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes from scratch.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Functions: Cloud Functions is a serverless platform for running lightweight, event-driven code snippets, not for orchestrating complex containerized microservices.
why other options are wrong.App Engine Standard: App Engine Standard runs application code in specific language runtimes, not custom Docker containers requiring a container orchestration platform.

questions.questionText: You are creating a new Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Your team wants to completely eliminate the operational overhead of managing underlying compute nodes, scaling node pools, and upgrading operating systems. Which mode of operation should you select for your GKE cluster?

explanation.general explanation: GKE Autopilot is a mode of operation where Google manages the entire cluster infrastructure, including the worker nodes and node pools. You simply deploy your pods, and you only pay for the CPU and memory resources your pods request.

why other options are wrong.GKE Standard: In Standard mode, the customer is responsible for managing, scaling, and upgrading the underlying node pools (Compute Engine instances).
why other options are wrong.GKE on Bare Metal: This requires the customer to manage their own physical hardware and operating systems on-premises.
why other options are wrong.Anthos Service Mesh: Anthos Service Mesh manages traffic routing and security between microservices, but does not manage the underlying compute nodes of a cluster.

questions.questionText: Your GKE Standard cluster runs web applications on standard N2 machine types. Your data science team wants to deploy a new containerized application that requires high-performance GPUs. How should you provision compute resources within the existing cluster to support this new application?
options: Create a new Node Pool within the cluster specifying machine types with attached GPUs.
Upgrade the entire existing Node Pool to machines with attached GPUs.
Create a new GKE cluster exclusively for the GPU workloads.
Change the configuration of the GKE Control Plane to enable GPU processing.
correctAnswers: Create a new Node Pool within the cluster specifying machine types with attached GPUs.

explanation.general explanation: In GKE Standard, a cluster can have multiple Node Pools. A Node Pool is a group of nodes within a cluster that all have the same configuration. Creating a new Node Pool with GPUs allows you to run specialized workloads on the same cluster without forcing expensive GPUs on the standard web apps.

why other options are wrong.Upgrade the entire existing Node Pool to: This would attach expensive GPUs to the standard web applications that do not need them, significantly increasing costs.
why other options are wrong.Create a new GKE cluster exclusively for: While possible, it adds management overhead to run a second cluster when a single cluster with multiple node pools can handle diverse workloads.
why other options are wrong.Change the configuration of the GKE Cont: The Control Plane is managed by Google and does not execute the actual application containers; worker nodes execute the workloads.

questions.questionText: Your containerized application is deployed on GKE. During a sudden spike in traffic, Kubernetes schedules new pods, but they remain in a 'Pending' state because the existing worker nodes lack available CPU and memory. Which feature should you enable to automatically provision additional VMs to host these pending pods?

explanation.general explanation: The GKE Cluster Autoscaler automatically resizes the number of underlying nodes (VMs) in a given node pool based on the demands of your workloads. When pods cannot be scheduled due to a lack of resources, it provisions new nodes.

why other options are wrong.Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): HPA increases or decreases the number of *pods*, not the underlying physical nodes.
why other options are wrong.Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): VPA adjusts the CPU and memory limits of individual *pods*, not the underlying physical nodes.
why other options are wrong.Managed Instance Group (MIG) Autoscaling: While GKE uses MIGs under the hood, you must use the GKE-specific Cluster Autoscaler so it integrates correctly with the Kubernetes scheduler.

questions.questionText: You are configuring a deployment in GKE. You want Kubernetes to automatically increase the number of running replicas (pods) when the average CPU utilization of the deployment exceeds 70%. Which Kubernetes resource must you configure?

explanation.general explanation: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) automatically updates a workload resource (like a Deployment) to increase or decrease the number of pods to match demand, commonly based on observed average CPU utilization.

why other options are wrong.Cluster Autoscaler: Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes physical VMs (nodes) in the cluster, not application pods.
why other options are wrong.Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): VPA adjusts the size (CPU/memory requests and limits) of individual pods, rather than creating more replicas.
why other options are wrong.ReplicaSet: A ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of pod replicas are running, but it does not automatically scale them up or down based on metrics like CPU; HPA manages the ReplicaSet count.

questions.questionText: Your containerized web application is hosted on Google Cloud. The application needs to automatically scale from 0 to 1000 instances based on HTTP requests, and your team does not want to manage any Kubernetes clusters, nodes, or pod manifests. Which service is the most appropriate?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Run is a fully managed, serverless platform specifically designed to run stateless containers that are invocable via HTTP requests. It completely abstracts infrastructure management and natively scales to zero when there is no traffic.

why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Standard: GKE requires managing clusters, node pools, and writing Kubernetes YAML manifests.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Managed Instance Groups: MIGs manage raw VMs, not serverless containers, and require significant infrastructure management.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Functions: While serverless and able to scale to zero, Cloud Functions are for executing single-purpose code snippets, not for running arbitrary Docker containers hosting full web applications.

questions.questionText: To expose your GKE web application to the public internet using a Google Cloud External HTTP(S) Load Balancer, which Kubernetes object must you create to configure the routing rules and bind to the load balancer?

explanation.general explanation: In GKE, creating an Ingress object automatically provisions and configures a Google Cloud External HTTP(S) Load Balancer. It defines the routing rules for external HTTP and HTTPS traffic to reach the backend services within your cluster.

why other options are wrong.Service type NodePort: NodePort exposes the service on each Node's IP at a static port. It does not provision an L7 External HTTP(S) Load Balancer.
why other options are wrong.Service type ClusterIP: ClusterIP exposes the service on a cluster-internal IP, making it entirely inaccessible from the external internet.
why other options are wrong.StatefulSet: A StatefulSet manages the deployment and scaling of stateful applications (like databases), not network routing.

questions.questionText: You are building a CI/CD pipeline for your GKE workloads. After Cloud Build compiles your application into a Docker container image, where is the recommended, fully managed Google Cloud location to securely store this image before GKE pulls it?

explanation.general explanation: Artifact Registry is the recommended, fully managed Google Cloud service for storing, managing, and securing container images and language packages. GKE securely pulls container images directly from Artifact Registry.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage: While Artifact Registry uses Cloud Storage under the hood, you do not push or pull Docker images directly to/from Cloud Storage buckets using Docker commands.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Persistent Disk: Persistent Disks provide block storage for individual VMs, not centralized container image registry services.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Source Repositories: Cloud Source Repositories store source code (like Git), not compiled Docker container images.

questions.questionText: Your application running in a GKE pod needs to securely read files from a Cloud Storage bucket. Following Google Cloud security best practices, how should you grant the pod access to the Cloud Storage API without downloading JSON service account keys?
options: Assign a Cloud IAM Service Account to the underlying Compute Engine Node.
Store the Service Account JSON key in a Kubernetes Secret.
Use Workload Identity to bind a Kubernetes Service Account to a Google Cloud IAM Service Account.
Make the Cloud Storage bucket publicly readable.
correctAnswers: Use Workload Identity to bind a Kubernetes Service Account to a Google Cloud IAM Service Account.

explanation.general explanation: Workload Identity is the recommended way to authenticate GKE workloads to Google Cloud services. It links a Kubernetes Service Account (KSA) to a Google Cloud Service Account (GSA), allowing pods to securely access APIs without managing vulnerable JSON keys.

why other options are wrong.Assign a Cloud IAM Service Account to th: This violates the principle of least privilege, as every pod running on that node would inherit the permissions to access the bucket.
why other options are wrong.Store the Service Account JSON key in a: Downloading and managing long-lived JSON keys is an anti-pattern and a security risk.
why other options are wrong.Make the Cloud Storage bucket publicly r: This exposes your potentially sensitive data to the entire internet.

questions.questionText: To ensure your GKE cluster provides High Availability (HA) against a data center outage, you want the Kubernetes control plane and the worker nodes to be distributed across multiple physical zones within a region. What type of GKE cluster should you create?

explanation.general explanation: A Regional GKE cluster distributes its control plane replicas and worker nodes across multiple zones within a given region. This ensures the cluster survives a single zonal (data center) failure.

why other options are wrong.A Zonal cluster: A Zonal cluster has a single control plane situated in one specific zone; if that zone fails, the cluster is unmanageable.
why other options are wrong.An Autopilot cluster: While Autopilot clusters are Regional by default, 'Regional' is the specific architectural term defining the cross-zone topology for HA.
why other options are wrong.A Private cluster: A Private cluster ensures nodes only have internal IP addresses for security; it does not define the geographic availability topology.

questions.questionText: Your team is deploying a distributed database (like Cassandra) into GKE. Each pod requires a persistent identity, a stable network hostname, and its own dedicated persistent volume that survives pod restarts. Which Kubernetes resource must you use?

explanation.general explanation: StatefulSets are used for managing stateful applications in Kubernetes. They provide guarantees about the ordering and uniqueness of pods, ensuring each pod maintains a persistent identity (e.g., db-0, db-1) and stable storage across restarts.

why other options are wrong.Deployment: Deployments are designed for stateless applications. Pods are treated as interchangeable and do not maintain a stable network identity.
why other options are wrong.ReplicaSet: ReplicaSets maintain a stable set of replica Pods but do not offer the stable identities and dedicated volume mapping of a StatefulSet.
why other options are wrong.DaemonSet: DaemonSets ensure that all (or some) Nodes run a copy of a specific Pod (like a logging agent), not for deploying ordered, stateful database nodes.

questions.questionText: You are running a highly fault-tolerant, batch data processing workload on GKE. You want to significantly reduce the compute costs associated with running these pods. Which GKE node pool configuration should you implement?
options: Create a Node Pool using Spot VMs (Preemptible VMs).
Create a Node Pool using Sole-tenant nodes.
correctAnswers: Create a Node Pool using Spot VMs (Preemptible VMs).

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs (formerly Preemptible VMs) offer highly discounted compute capacity (up to 91% off) but can be terminated by Google at any time. Because the workload is fault-tolerant and batch-oriented, it can survive these interruptions, making Spot VMs the perfect cost-optimization strategy.

why other options are wrong.Create a Node Pool using Sole-tenant nod: Sole-tenant nodes provide dedicated physical hardware for compliance and are significantly more expensive.
VPA optimizes resource requests but does not inherently provide massive compute discounts like Spot VMs do.
why other options are wrong.Use memory-optimized custom machine type: Memory-optimized machines are among the most expensive instances and are meant for large in-memory databases, not cost-saving batch jobs.

questions.questionText: A best practice in container orchestration is to separate application configuration data from the container image itself, allowing you to use the same image across dev, staging, and production environments. Which Kubernetes resource allows you to inject configuration data into a pod at runtime?

explanation.general explanation: A ConfigMap is an API object used to store non-confidential data in key-value pairs. Pods can consume ConfigMaps as environment variables, command-line arguments, or as configuration files in a volume, successfully decoupling environment-specific configuration from container images.

why other options are wrong.Ingress: Ingress manages external HTTP/S routing to services.
why other options are wrong.PersistentVolumeClaim: PVCs request physical storage volumes for data persistence, not configuration parameter injection.
why other options are wrong.ReplicaSet: ReplicaSets maintain the desired number of pod replicas, not configuration data.

questions.questionText: You want to ensure your GKE cluster is automatically upgraded to the latest stable Kubernetes version without manual intervention. Which feature should you configure?

explanation.general explanation: GKE Release Channels (Rapid, Regular, Stable) allow you to enroll your cluster in a Google-managed upgrade strategy. Google automatically upgrades the cluster's control plane and nodes based on the cadence of the channel you select.

why other options are wrong.Cluster Autoscaler: The Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes compute nodes based on load; it does not perform version upgrades.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Build triggers: Cloud Build automates CI/CD application deployments, not infrastructure version upgrades.
why other options are wrong.Anthos Config Management: This synchronizes Kubernetes manifests and RBAC rules across clusters from Git; it does not upgrade the GKE version itself.

questions.questionText: Your enterprise organization needs a single platform to manage Kubernetes clusters deployed in Google Cloud, in an on-premises data center, and in AWS. Which Google Cloud solution provides this multi-cloud container orchestration management?

explanation.general explanation: GKE Enterprise (formerly Anthos) is Google Cloud's hybrid and multi-cloud platform. It allows organizations to build, deploy, and manage Kubernetes-based applications consistently across Google Cloud, on-premises data centers, and other public clouds like AWS or Azure.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Run: Cloud Run is a managed serverless platform that runs exclusively within Google Cloud.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine: Compute Engine provides VMs inside Google Cloud, not multi-cloud Kubernetes orchestration.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Endpoints: Cloud Endpoints is an API management system, not a container orchestration platform.

questions.questionText: Your developers commit code to a Git repository. You need a fully managed CI/CD service on Google Cloud that can automatically build a Docker container image from that code and push it to Artifact Registry. Which service should you use?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Build is a fully managed continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) platform. It executes builds on Google Cloud infrastructure and is natively designed to compile source code into Docker containers and push them to Artifact Registry.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Run: Cloud Run runs containers; it does not build them from source code.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Deploy: Cloud Deploy automates the continuous delivery (CD) of applications to target environments like GKE, but relies on Cloud Build (CI) to actually build the container image first.
why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine: GKE is the runtime environment that orchestrates containers, it does not build the images.

questions.questionText: You are deploying a stateless REST API to GKE. You want Kubernetes to ensure that exactly 5 replicas of your application are running at all times, and that failing pods are automatically replaced. Which Kubernetes resource should you create?

explanation.general explanation: A Deployment provides declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. You define a desired state (e.g., 5 replicas), and the Deployment Controller changes the actual state to the desired state, automatically replacing any pods that fail.

why other options are wrong.Pod: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit. Creating a single Pod does not provide replication or self-healing if the node dies.
why other options are wrong.ConfigMap: A ConfigMap holds configuration data, not application replica definitions.
why other options are wrong.Service: A Service provides network exposure and load balancing across pods, but it does not manage the creation or replication of the pods themselves.

questions.questionText: Your application deployed in GKE consists of a frontend Deployment and a backend database Deployment. Because the backend pods are ephemeral and their IP addresses constantly change, how do you provide a single, stable internal IP address for the frontend to connect to the backend?
options: Create a Kubernetes Service (type ClusterIP) for the backend pods.
Assign Static External IPs to the backend pods.
Create an Ingress object for the backend pods.
Use a Kubernetes StatefulSet for the frontend.
correctAnswers: Create a Kubernetes Service (type ClusterIP) for the backend pods.

explanation.general explanation: A Kubernetes Service (specifically type ClusterIP) provides a stable internal IP address and DNS name that load balances traffic across a dynamic set of backend pods. This allows the frontend to easily connect to the backend without worrying about changing pod IPs.

why other options are wrong.Assign Static External IPs to the backen: Backend databases should not have external IPs for security reasons, and assigning static IPs to ephemeral pods defeats the purpose of orchestration.
why other options are wrong.Create an Ingress object for the backend: Ingress is used to route external HTTP(S) traffic from outside the cluster, not for internal service-to-service communication.
why other options are wrong.Use a Kubernetes StatefulSet for the fro: The frontend is stateless, and changing its deployment type doesn't solve the problem of locating the backend database.

questions.questionText: Your GKE cluster is undergoing an automated node upgrade. You want to guarantee that your highly available web application always maintains at least 3 running replicas during the node disruption, preventing the cluster from evicting all your pods simultaneously. What should you configure?

explanation.general explanation: A Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from voluntary disruptions (like node upgrades or draining). It ensures that a minimum available number of replicas (e.g., 3) is always maintained.

why other options are wrong.A Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): VPA adjusts pod resource sizing, it does not prevent pod eviction during node maintenance.
why other options are wrong.A Cluster Autoscaler: The Cluster Autoscaler scales physical nodes; it respects PDBs but does not enforce minimum pod availability constraints itself.

questions.questionText: When using GKE Standard, Kubernetes consists of a Control Plane and Worker Nodes. Under the Google Cloud shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching, managing, and backing up the Kubernetes Control Plane (API server, etcd, scheduler)?

explanation.general explanation: In Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Google Cloud fully manages the control plane. This includes the API server, scheduler, and the etcd key-value store. Google handles patching, backing up, and scaling these components.

why other options are wrong.The Customer: The customer is only responsible for managing the worker nodes in GKE Standard (or nothing in GKE Autopilot), not the control plane.
why other options are wrong.Third-party integrators: Google manages the control plane directly.
why other options are wrong.The Kubernetes Open Source Community: The community develops the software, but Google operates and maintains the managed service.

questions.questionText: To improve security within your GKE cluster, you want to restrict which pods can communicate with each other. For example, you want to ensure the 'frontend' pods can only communicate with the 'backend' pods, and nothing else. Which Kubernetes feature should you implement?

explanation.general explanation: Kubernetes Network Policies allow you to specify how groups of pods are allowed to communicate with each other and other network endpoints. They act as application-level firewalls inside the cluster.

why other options are wrong.VPC Firewall Rules: VPC Firewall rules operate at the VM (node) network level. Because multiple pods share a node, VPC firewalls cannot easily restrict pod-to-pod communication within the same cluster.
why other options are wrong.Workload Identity: Workload identity manages authentication to Google Cloud APIs, not internal pod-to-pod network traffic.
why other options are wrong.ConfigMaps: ConfigMaps store configuration data, not security rules.

questions.questionText: You are migrating a containerized application to Google Cloud. The application runs a background task indefinitely and requires raw access to the host's networking namespace. It cannot be run as a serverless workload. Which container orchestration service allows you the necessary control over the underlying nodes to support this?

explanation.general explanation: GKE Standard allows you full access and control over the underlying Compute Engine worker nodes. If an application requires specialized configurations like host networking access or privileged containers, GKE Standard provides the flexibility required.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Run: Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform. It abstracts away the host and does not allow access to the host network namespace.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Functions: Cloud Functions execute code snippets in a highly restricted sandbox, not suitable for long-running host-level tasks.
why other options are wrong.App Engine Standard: App Engine provides a PaaS sandbox and does not support arbitrary Docker containers requiring host-level access.

questions.questionText: By default, when you create a modern GKE cluster, it utilizes Alias IPs so that pods are assigned native IP addresses directly from the VPC subnet. What is this network architecture called in GKE?

explanation.general explanation: A VPC-native cluster uses Alias IPs to assign pod IP addresses from a secondary range on the VPC subnet. This makes pod IPs natively routable within the Google Cloud VPC without requiring custom static routes.

why other options are wrong.Routes-based cluster: Routes-based clusters (the older, legacy method) rely on custom static routes in the VPC to direct traffic to nodes for pod IP ranges.
why other options are wrong.Private cluster: A Private cluster means the nodes lack external IP addresses; it is independent of whether the cluster is VPC-native or routes-based.
why other options are wrong.Shared VPC cluster: Shared VPC is a network construct that allows multiple projects to use a single VPC. A cluster in a Shared VPC must be VPC-native, but 'VPC-native' is the core term for the Alias IP behavior.

questions.questionText: You need to perform manual maintenance on a GKE worker node and must shut it down. Before shutting it down, what command should you use to gracefully evict the running pods so they are rescheduled onto other active nodes?

explanation.general explanation: The `kubectl drain` command safely evicts all pods from a node and marks the node as unschedulable (cordons it). This allows the Kubernetes scheduler to gracefully recreate the pods on other healthy nodes before you perform maintenance.

why other options are wrong.`kubectl stop node`: This is not a valid Kubernetes command.
why other options are wrong.`gcloud container clusters resize`: This command changes the size of a node pool, which might randomly delete a node without warning, causing disruption.
why other options are wrong.`kubectl delete pods --all`: This violently deletes all pods on all nodes, causing a massive outage across the cluster.

questions.questionText: To increase security, you want to ensure that the worker nodes in your GKE cluster are protected against rootkits and boot-level malware. Which GKE feature should you enable?

explanation.general explanation: Shielded GKE Nodes provide strong, verifiable node identity and integrity to increase the security of GKE nodes. They leverage Secure Boot, virtual trusted platform modules (vTPM), and integrity monitoring to protect against boot-level rootkits.

why other options are wrong.Binary Authorization: Binary Authorization ensures only trusted, signed container images are deployed to GKE. It protects the application layer, not the boot process of the underlying VM node.
why other options are wrong.Network Policies: These restrict traffic between pods, not boot-level node security.
why other options are wrong.Workload Identity: This provides secure access to GCP APIs for pods, not node-level boot security.

questions.questionText: Which three autoscaling mechanisms are natively available and commonly used within Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to scale workloads and infrastructure?

explanation.general explanation: GKE supports three main autoscaling dimensions: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (adds/removes pods), Vertical Pod Autoscaler (adjusts CPU/RAM of pods), and Cluster Autoscaler (adds/removes physical worker nodes in the cluster).

why other options are wrong.App Engine Autoscaler: App Engine is a completely separate PaaS service and its autoscaler does not manage GKE.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Run Autoscaler: Cloud Run is a separate serverless container service; its scaling mechanisms are independent of GKE.

questions.questionText: When deciding between GKE Standard and GKE Autopilot, which two characteristics apply exclusively to GKE Autopilot?
options: Google fully manages and provisions the underlying compute nodes.
You pay per pod based on requested CPU, memory, and storage.
You must manually configure SSH access to the worker nodes.
You pay for the underlying Compute Engine instances regardless of whether pods are running.
correctAnswers: Google fully manages and provisions the underlying compute nodes.
You pay per pod based on requested CPU, memory, and storage.

explanation.general explanation: In GKE Autopilot, Google entirely abstracts the infrastructure, meaning Google provisions and manages the compute nodes. Additionally, the billing model changes: you only pay for the exact resources (CPU/RAM) your scheduled pods request, rather than paying for the entire node's capacity.

why other options are wrong.You must manually configure SSH access t: Autopilot removes SSH access to nodes to maintain security and managed service guarantees.
why other options are wrong.You pay for the underlying Compute Engin: This describes the billing model of GKE Standard, where you pay for the VM capacity.

questions.questionText: Which two Kubernetes resources can be used to expose an application running in a GKE cluster to external users on the internet?

explanation.general explanation: To expose an application externally in GKE, you can use an Ingress object (which provisions an External HTTP(S) Load Balancer for Layer 7 routing) or a Service of type LoadBalancer (which provisions a Network Load Balancer for Layer 4 TCP/UDP traffic).

why other options are wrong.Service of type ClusterIP: ClusterIP is the default service type and only exposes the service on an internal IP address reachable only from within the cluster.
why other options are wrong.ConfigMap: A ConfigMap is used for storing configuration variables, not for networking or exposing applications.

questions.questionText: If your development team has containerized their microservices using Docker, which two Google Cloud compute services can natively execute those container images?

explanation.general explanation: Both Cloud Run (a fully managed serverless platform) and Google Kubernetes Engine (a managed Kubernetes orchestration platform) are designed to natively execute and scale Docker container images.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage: Cloud Storage is an object storage service. It stores files, but it provides no compute capabilities to run or execute containers.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Spanner: Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database service. It is not a platform for running customer application containers.

questions.questionText: When provisioning a GKE Standard cluster, the architecture is divided into two primary parts. Which two components make up the high-level architecture of a standard Kubernetes cluster?

explanation.general explanation: The fundamental architecture of a Kubernetes cluster consists of the Control Plane (the master components that manage the cluster, like the API server and scheduler) and the Worker Nodes (the virtual machines that actually run the containerized applications/pods).

why other options are wrong.The Cloud CDN edge nodes: Cloud CDN is a content delivery network used to cache static assets; it is not a structural component of a Kubernetes cluster.
why other options are wrong.The Artifact Registry: Artifact Registry stores the container images before they are deployed, but it is an external storage service, not an active part of the cluster's internal orchestration architecture.
